parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Picture the electron velocity arrow in Fig. 8.1 and split it into two parts - one along the field lines and one across them. Which side of that right-angled triangle is the normal component?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Resolve The Velocity Into Components**
Think of the incoming velocity as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. One side is parallel to the $B$-field, the other side is normal (at $90^{\circ}$) to the $B$-field. You need the side opposite the $30^{\circ}$ angle.

Step 2: **Calculate The Normal Component**
For an angle $\theta$ to the field direction:
$$v_N = v \sin\theta$$
$$v_N = (3.4 \times 10^{7}) \times \sin 30^{\circ}$$
$$v_N = (3.4 \times 10^{7}) \times 0.5 = 1.7 \times 10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: The normal component of velocity is at $90^{\circ}$ to the field, so the magnetic force on it acts as a centripetal force bending it into a circle. What two expressions for force must be set equal here?
Hint 2: Rearrange the force balance to make radius $r$ the subject, using only $m$, $v_N$, $B$ and $q$. Remember to convert $B$ from mT to T.
Hint 3: Use electron values $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$ and $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ with your $v_N$ from (a)(i) to evaluate $r$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set Magnetic Force Equal To Centripetal Force**
Only the velocity normal to the field feels a force. That force is always perpendicular to $v_N$, so it acts as the centripetal force for circular motion:
$$\frac{mv_N^{2}}{r} = Bqv_N$$

Step 2: **Rearrange For Radius**
Cancel one $v_N$ to get the standard result:
$$r = \frac{mv_N}{Bq}$$
This makes sense - faster particles make wider circles, stronger fields bend them tighter.

Step 3: **Substitute Values With Correct Units**
Convert flux density: $B = 3.2 \text{ mT} = 3.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$. Use $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$, $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $v_N = 1.7 \times 10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$r = \frac{(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(1.7 \times 10^{7})}{(3.2 \times 10^{-3})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})}$$
$$r \approx 0.030 \text{ m}$$

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: zero force for motion parallel to field
hints: Hint 1: Recall that magnetic force depends on the angle between velocity and field. What is that angle for the component along the field direction?
parts.proper_answer: Zero, no force acts due to the parallel component.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply The Angle Rule For Magnetic Force**
Magnetic force is $F = Bqv\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $v$ and $B$. For the parallel component, $v$ is along $B$, so $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ and $\sin 0^{\circ} = 0$.
$$F = 0$$
So the parallel component just carries on unchanged at constant velocity, with no deflection.

parts.label: (c)
key_concepts: superposition of circular and linear motion
hints: Hint 1: Combine your two earlier ideas - (a) gives circling across the field and (b) gives steady drift along the field. What 3D shape do you get when you add a circle to a forward motion?
parts.proper_answer: The electron follows a helical (coil / corkscrew) path along the field direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combine The Two Motions**
Across the field you have uniform circular motion from (a), and along the field you have uniform straight-line motion with no force from (b). Adding them together, the circle moves forward as time goes on.
This produces a helix - like a coil or corkscrew - wound around the direction of the magnetic field.
